SEOUL, Oct 28 : South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix reported a more than seven-fold rise in quarterly operating profit to a record high on Wednesday, beating market forecasts, as continued demand for AI infrastructure drove up memory chip prices. The Nvidia supplier also said it will pursue shareholder returns totalling about 100 trillion won ($75.4 billion) this year, comprising cash dividends of 30 trillion won and share repurchases and cancellations of 60 trillion won, including 40 trillion won announced in August. SK Hynix also reiterated that it expects demand to continue to exceed supply through 2030. To improve mid-to-long term demand visibility, SK Hynix has signed long-term agreements (LTAs) with 14 major customers, while "proactively discussing with a number of customers the possibility of extending the contract terms, which are typically five years."

That compared with the 76.7 trillion won LSEG SmartEstimate, which is weighted toward estimates from analysts who are more consistently accurate. Oct 27 : Robinhood Markets missed Wall Street estimates for third-quarter profit on Tuesday, as slower cryptocurrency trading and higher expenses overshadowed strong activity in options and prediction markets. Shares of the Menlo Park, California-based company fell 7 per cent in after-hours trading. The trading platform's transaction-based revenue from cryptocurrencies fell 55 per cent to $120 million from a year earlier. Crypto markets have come under pressure this year amid heightened volatility and persistent outflows, as inflationary pressures and higher interest rates make bonds and other traditional investments more attractive than speculative assets.

Bitcoin, the world's largest cryptocurrency, has fallen as much as 8 per cent year to date as geopolitical tensions and rising oil prices add to market uncertainty. OPTIONS, EVENT CONTRACTS OFFSET CRYPTO SLUMP Robinhood's overall transaction-based revenue rose about 19 per cent to $867 million, driven by a more than sixfold increase in event-contracts revenue and a 31 per cent jump in options revenue. However, revenue growth lagged the increase in trading contracts, suggesting that growth was becoming more concentrated in a few key areas, said Bill Birmingham, research head at REX Financial. "Prediction markets are becoming a second outlet for the same core active traders rather than a funnel for new customers," Birmingham said, adding that some of the volume may reflect a shift from existing trading activity rather than incremental business. Robinhood CFO Shiv Verma, however, emphasized that prediction markets was an important growth driver for the company. "Prediction markets is almost a $500-million-a-year business already, and so growing incredibly nicely, and it's less than two years old because it came out at the start of the 2024 election," Verma told journalists over a call. He said both sports and non-sports event contracts were growing strongly, with non-sports contracts accounting for a larger share of overall trading volume. The company's operating expenses rose 16 per cent to $739 million for the three months ended September 30, driven by higher credit-loss provisions, spending on new businesses such as Trump Accounts and Rothera, and increased marketing. Robinhood posted a profit of 51 cents per share, missing analysts' expectations of a per-share profit of 55 cents, according to estimates compiled by LSEG.

Source: Reuters

Oct 27 : Visa beat expectations for fourth-quarter results on Tuesday as customers continued swiping their cards to pay for travel, shopping and dining out despite macroeconomic uncertainty. The results from the world's largest payments processor underscore a robust US economy in the face of persistent inflationary pressures as consumers continue spending, underpinned by a strong labor market and wage growth. "Growth across consumer spend bands remained relatively consistent with prior quarters, with the highest spend band continuing to grow the fastest. We did not see signs of the lower spend consumer weakening in our volumes," Visa finance chief Chris Suh said in a post-earnings call. Payments volume, a gauge of consumer and business spending on Visa's network, jumped 9 per cent in the reported quarter on a constant-dollar basis, while processed transactions rose 10 per cent.

Visa's extensive digital payments network, which spans more than 200 countries and territories, positions it to better endure economic downturns as billions of people globally rely on the card network for everyday spending and other purchases. CLIENT INCENTIVES, PROFIT FORECAST IN FOCUS Client incentives jumped 21 per cent to $5.1 billion in the quarter from the prior year, largely driven by new deals that were signed during the July to September period and early in the fourth quarter. "The one thing to nitpick is client incentives, which were above expectations," Seaport analyst Jeff Cantwell said, adding the development likely impacted Visa's fiscal 2027 forecasts. Suh told analysts incentives growth would step up in fiscal 2027 as Visa is expecting around 25 per cent of its payments volumes to be renewed, including with several large clients. That compares with 20 per cent in fiscal 2026. The company anticipates fiscal 2027 profit per share growth between a low-double-digit and low-teens percentage, while net revenue growth is expected to be in the low-double-digit percentage. "While some may be underwhelmed by the EPS guide, we think it likely reflects... (the management's) decision to keep investing in long-term strategic initiatives to extend the durability of top-line growth," KBW analysts led by Sanjay Sakhrani said. Visa's shares fell about 1.4 per cent in extended trading. The stock has gained 14.6 per cent this year through the last close. On an adjusted basis, it earned $3.48 per share in the three months ended September 30, beating an expectation of $3.44 per share, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. CROSS-BORDER STRENGTH Cross-border volumes excluding intra-Europe, a measure of international travel demand, were a bright spot as they jumped 14 per cent in the quarter on a constant-dollar basis. "It is reflective of strong consumer sentiment, strong demand for travel experiences, and the fact that e-commerce has also just expanded," Suh said. Suh told Reuters travel in and out of the Middle East was also coming back closer to normal levels after being suppressed due to the Iran conflict. The FIFA World Cup, which ran from June 11 to July 19, has also helped boost activity across Visa's network as it brought many visitors to the United States. "XB (cross-border) showed a nice step-up in growth sequentially, and that was one area we were watching for signs of potential weakness going into earnings," Seaport's Cantwell said. Net revenue jumped 13 per cent to $12.1 billion in the quarter. For fiscal year 2026, Visa hauled record net revenue of $46 billion. Rival Mastercard is set to report quarterly earnings later this week.

Source: Reuters

ZURICH, Oct 27 : Logitech International on Tuesday reported a better-than-expected profit for the second quarter, with the computer mouse and keyboard maker seeing higher demand for its gaming and video conferencing devices. The Swiss-U.S. company reported non-GAAP operating income of $231 million for the three months to the end of September, beating forecasts for $204 million in a consensus gathered by Visible Alpha and the company's own guidance for $185 million to $210 million. Sales rose 3 per cent to $1.22 billion, in line with analyst forecasts and towards the upper end of the company's own outlook of $1.19 billion to $1.22 billion. CEO Hanneke Faber said Logitech had come through a difficult period marked by tight component sourcing, higher costs and the conflict in the Middle East.

"Even as global PC shipments declined by 20 per cent in the quarter, our pointing devices and keyboards grew by mid single digits, demonstrating our growth opportunity comes from the large installed PC base," she told analysts on a call. Innovation, including products like matcha and latte-coloured mice, had helped the company grow sales in that category, while 15 new products in the gaming category boosted sales there. Sales of video collaboration equipment rose 12 per cent as business customers refreshed their workplaces after encouraging staff back to the office. "Video collaboration demand is strong and we expect it to continue to be strong," Faber said. "It's not discretionary. You need to refresh those rooms, you need expanded office space if you are going to ask people to come back to work." Faber said there was strong demand from healthcare and government customers. Logitech also said it had suffered a lower-than-expected impact from the forced closure at a factory of one of its semiconductor suppliers at the end of June, which it originally expected to cost it up to $200 million in lost sales in the next quarter. After getting chips from other suppliers, the company said it now expects the impact to be $70 million to $80 million. Logitech said its sales would be in the range of $1.36 billion to $1.43 billion for the three months to the end of December. It also expects non-GAAP operating income of $220 million to $255 million down from $312 million a year earlier, due to higher component and transport costs, as well as the lost sales caused by the factory shutdown.

Source: Reuters

LOS ANGELES, Oct 27 : UPS CEO Carol Tome told Reuters on Tuesday the AI data center boom is a decades-long opportunity for the world's largest parcel delivery and logistics company, which aims to boost profits by handling fewer, but more premium, shipments.   Global data center spending is estimated to hit roughly $1 trillion in 2026 and more than double before the end of the decade as tech giants like Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon invest billions of dollars in artificial intelligence facilities, which require significant new electricity infrastructure to power and cool servers and computer chips.  The logistics opportunity associated with data centers is $15 billion per year, said Tome.  "It is from manufacturing floor to front door," she said. UPS is flying in critical components such as advanced microprocessors, arranging ocean shipments for equipment of all shapes and sizes, warehousing goods and delivering parts to project sites.

Tome spoke after UPS raised its annual revenue and profit forecasts on better-than-expected third-quarter earnings. Data center projects have become divisive as communities weigh job creation and economic growth against electricity prices, water use and noise. Investors separately are questioning companies' massive investments in them. Nevertheless, there are many projects underway and once those are built, there will continue to be demand for parts and equipment to keep them running, Tome said. "This is something that's going to be decades," Tome said of demand. While UPS data center revenue is growing quickly, it has not yet matched revenue from its healthcare segment, which hit $3 billion in the latest quarter, Tome said, declining to give a figure for the newer business. INFLECTION POINT As part of Tome's "better, not bigger" growth strategy, UPS has been reconfiguring its network to be smaller, nimbler and more profitable.  It has consolidated facilities to reduce costs and improved service quality by investing in things like temperature sensors as well as package scanning and tracking. It also has focused on high-growth and high-margin segments like healthcare, returns and, most recently, data centers.   UPS has made significant headway in specialized healthcare logistics, shipping temperature-controlled chemotherapy drugs, cancer treatments and direct-to-consumer GLP-1 weight-loss drugs. It is now the largest player in the $148 billion global healthcare market after some key acquisitions and internal growth.    That business generated revenue of $6 billion for UPS in 2020 and is forecast to reach $13 billion in revenue this year, Tome said.   UPS is racing rival FedEx for the same high-margin volume as they each wean off low-margin to unprofitable deliveries of online purchases and other goods. FedEx, which has set up a dedicated team to court data center-related business, will report quarterly results after the market close on Wednesday. Meanwhile, retailers like Amazon.com  and Walmart as well as growing rivals like OnTrac are aggressively targeting domestic shipments in certain parts of the country. Some of that includes volume UPS and FedEx don't want.  UPS has cut doorstep deliveries of millions of packages for Amazon that it considered unprofitable, which helped lift its margin. Tome said the margin would keep improving every year. "We've moved through an important inflection point," Tome said.

Source: Reuters

FAST

NEW YORK, Oct 27 : The US Federal Election Commission's website has been targeted by a hacker or hackers, according to an email seen by Reuters, disrupting the agency's electronic filings system a week before the November 3 elections. The cyberattack comes as so-called super PACs and dark money groups spend record sums in the final days of the races. The elections will determine whether President Donald Trump's Republicans maintain their majorities in Congress for the next two years.  In a statement, the FEC said, "at this time, the FEC’s electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service." The FEC, which tracks the spending of candidates and political committees, said users could still search the website for past reports. It declined further comment on the outage. The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.

The outage prevents organizations from filing the FEC's 24-hour and 48-hour spending reports, which show how much political groups and others are spending on specific races. "I've never seen this in 26 years," said Steven Mele, president and CEO at political finance compliance firm MBA Consulting Group. "The result is there will be less disclosure on the elections" until it's fixed.  A status message posted by the FEC said its filing system had been down since around 10 p.m. ET on Monday (0200 GMT Tuesday). The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency referred questions to the FEC. The FBI did not immediately return messages seeking comment. The FEC posted the notice after campaign finance officers couldn't file mandatory reports late on Monday.  "We have a bad actor attempting to breach FEC systems. As a result, we’ve had to temporarily shut down our web facing services," an FEC electronic filings officer said in the email to several campaign compliance firms that night.  The midterms are now the most expensive US election in history with roughly $11.21 billion spent on advertising and future reservations so far, according to political ad tracker AdImpact. It's surpassed the previous record set in the 2024 elections when $11.2 billion was spent on all races, including $3.2 billion on the presidential race between Trump and former Vice President Kamala Harris, AdImpact said.  Much of the spending is being driven by super PACs, which can accept unlimited amounts of money from wealthy individuals and corporations and spend as much as they want on campaigns with few restrictions.  The sums being spent in recent weeks are staggering as Democrats gain ground in several Republican strongholds. Super PACs and dark money groups have spent an average of over $50 million per day over the last week, said Brendan Glavin, research director at nonpartisan campaign watchdog group OpenSecrets. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added.  "It's a big deal," he said of the outage, which leaves voters in the dark until the filing system is back online.  "These are the key reports that tell us what is happening," Glavin said. "In the last days of the election this is the only way for us to keep track of where the money's being spent" and who's spending it.

Source: Reuters

FAST

Oct 27 : The Federal Communications Commission said on Tuesday it approved Amazon Leo’s $11.5 billion deal to acquire Globalstar as the retail giant's satellite arm seeks to build a communications network to compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon Leo has launched nearly 400 satellites since April 2025 and aims to deploy thousands of satellites in Earth's low orbit by 2029. Through the deal, Amazon adds Globalstar's two dozen satellites and its mobile-satellite spectrum. Amazon, which has committed to investing more than $10 billion in Leo, is preparing to roll out its commercial satellite services by the end of 2026, the FCC said. The FCC said the companies’ assets will boost Amazon Leo’s entry into the direct-to-device market and allow the satellite operator to offer fixed and mobile services. "The FCC has empowered Amazon Leo to deliver fast, next-gen satellite broadband services, increase competition, and help communities stay connected all across the country," FCC Chair Brendan Carr said.

Tech companies are pouring billions of dollars into capturing the lucrative market for satellite-based connectivity as they race to compete with Starlink's network of more than 11,000 satellites. Amazon praised the approval, saying it "brings us a step closer to bringing new connectivity capabilities to customers." Amazon in July sought approval from the FCC for up to 5,105 satellites. Direct-to-device satellite technology allows smartphones and other devices to connect directly to satellites. The FCC will vote on Thursday to advance a new auction of wireless spectrum to boost "direct-to-device" services. Globalstar currently powers satellite-based safety features such as Emergency SOS and Find My for Apple's iPhone and Apple Watch users. Amazon said earlier that it has signed an agreement with Apple to continue providing those services. Apple invested about $1.5 billion in Globalstar in 2024 to fund the expansion of its iPhone communication services, in a deal that also gave the tech giant a 20 per cent equity stake in Globalstar. Apple accounted for about 63 per cent of Globalstar's revenue last year and Amazon plans to acquire Apple's stake, the FCC said. Globalstar said late last year that a new, Apple-backed network under development would expand its footprint to 54 satellites, including a small number of backups, from the two dozen currently.

Source: Reuters

NEW YORK, Oct 27 : A US regulator is investigating whether prediction market operator Polymarket violated a 2022 enforcement deal in which it promised to ban US users from its main overseas platform, reviving an inquiry the agency shuttered last year without bringing charges, said two people familiar with the matter. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is probing whether Polymarket took sufficient steps to keep US users off the platform as part of a broader investigation it opened into the company earlier this year, the people said. One of the people said the scrutiny is focused on Polymarket's past controls and processes. The agency is examining Polymarket's controls for determining where customers are located, as well as its advertising activities in the United States, as part of that inquiry, the people said. Polymarket is based in New York and has an offshore entity registered in Panama.

The CFTC is also scrutinizing Polymarket's US platform, which the company began rolling out late last year, including its customer onboarding processes and customer protections, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss confidential enforcement issues. Reuters is reporting these elements of the probe for the first time. The Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg News and other media first reported in June that the CFTC was broadly probing Polymarket, but provided few details. Bloomberg added that the CFTC was looking into social media activity tied to the company. Spokespeople for the CFTC and Polymarket declined to comment. Probes are not necessarily an indication of wrongdoing and many do not result in enforcement action.  The new details, nevertheless, raise fresh questions over why the CFTC and Justice Department last year closed similar probes into whether Polymarket had violated the 2022 settlement, which resolved CFTC allegations at the time that Polymarket had been operating in the US unlawfully since its launch in 2020.  Neither agency has commented on the decision to close the probes and a Justice Department spokesperson declined to comment for this story. Prediction markets allow traders to bet on real-world events, including sports, government policy announcements and elections. Aided by supportive policies under President Donald Trump's second administration, the industry has surged over the past two years. Trump's son, Donald Trump Jr, is a Polymarket investor.  As the platforms have grown, they have drawn scrutiny from Democratic lawmakers and advocacy groups worried the platforms are creating new avenues for insider trading, while recent political upsets, including in Brazil this week, have raised questions about their accuracy. Polymarket has said it has revamped controls. The firm says it expressly prohibits the use of virtual private networks (VPNs) or similar tools to circumvent its geographic restrictions, and has extensive controls to monitor for misconduct and to prevent restricted users from accessing its offshore platform.  Speaking to Reuters in August, Shana Bautista, Polymarket's global head of investigations and intelligence, said US users circumventing its restrictions was not "a really prevalent issue."  BIDEN ADMINISTRATION AGENCIES OPENED PROBE IN 2024 Under the 2022 settlement negotiated by the CFTC's former Biden-era leadership, Polymarket agreed to stop offering its market to US users. But as 2024 US election bets on the platform grew, political pundits and social media users questioned whether Americans were circumventing Polymarket's restrictions.   Months before the election, the CFTC opened a probe into whether Polymarket was complying with the deal, Reuters and other media reported at the time. The Justice Department opened a related investigation, with the FBI searching Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan's New York home in November 2024. Two months later, the Trump administration took office and appointed new leaders to both agencies. On July 15, 2025, Coplan said in an X post that the CFTC and Justice Department had closed their probes and cleared the company of any wrongdoing. A week later, Polymarket said it had bought a CFTC-licensed derivatives exchange, which became the platform for its US operation. CFTC-registered platforms must comply with certain customer protection and market abuse prevention requirements. While CFTC data shows the agency's overall enforcement activity has slumped during Trump's second presidency, its enforcement director David Miller said during his first month on the job in March that he would aggressively police prediction markets.  In April, the agency and Justice Department charged a US soldier, alleging he made $400,000 from insider bets on Polymarket's offshore platform, sparking fresh questions about its controls.  According to the indictment, Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who has pleaded not guilty, accessed the platform using a VPN and "exit mode," which geolocated to a foreign country. Polymarket said at the time that it had referred the matter to the authorities.

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 27 : Oracle said on Tuesday it is expanding its cloud AI chip deals with Nvidia while also diversifying to add offerings from Nvidia rivals such as Alphabet's Google and Cerebras Systems. Oracle and Nvidia said the cloud firm will expand to "multi-gigawatt scale" with Nvidia's newest generation of "Vera Rubin" AI servers. The companies did not disclose the value of the deal, though Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has previously said that Vera Rubin systems can generate up to $40 billion in revenue per gigawatt for the chipmaker. Oracle is also diversifying its offerings, saying that even the Nvidia-based systems will skip some of Nvidia's networking chips in favor of Oracle's own in-house "Acceleron" networking chips. Oracle on Tuesday said it will begin offering Google's tensor processing unit (TPU) chips for the first time. "Different AI workloads have different compute needs," Mahesh Thiagarajan, president of Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, said in a statement. "That choice gives (customers) the flexibility to choose the right infrastructure for the performance, throughput and economics of each AI workload.”

While Nvidia dominates the market for training AI systems, the inference market is more competitive and diverse. "That's a massive expansion of our customer base of tier-one customers," Cerebras CEO Andrew Feldman said of the Oracle deal in an interview with Reuters. "We're being deployed in other people's data centers at large scale." Oracle, which plans to hold an investor day this week, did not disclose how it plans to finance the chip purchases. BENGALURU, Oct 27 : High inflation will persist in the global economy well into next year, according to hundreds of economists polled by Reuters, who are now increasingly concerned that price pressures will become entrenched beyond rising energy costs caused by the conflict in the Middle East. More than $1 trillion of investment in artificial intelligence technology globally since last year has made some economies more resilient at a time when cost of living pressures are squeezing households and shaping national politics. Most central banks have raised interest rates only a few times or not at all, but more could come if inflation pressures broaden. A global rout in bond markets in recent months has also tightened financial conditions through higher yields. Crude oil prices, which have stayed above $100 a barrel since October 7, hit a six-month high of over $117 last week and are up more than 60 per cent since the US-Israeli war with Iran began almost eight months ago.

Even forecasters who did not anticipate a quick end to the war are now sounding more concerned about inflation resurgence, particularly given the resilience of global growth. More than 500 economists Reuters surveyed globally this month raised their 2027 inflation forecasts for 31 of the 50 economies polled on and growth forecasts for 23 of them. "I am getting much more concerned about inflation again," said Janet Henry, global chief economist at HSBC. "The longer the situation evolves and escalates in the Middle East and the higher the broad basket of price pressures builds, the greater the likelihood that we get not just higher but more persistent inflation." Economists raised 2027 inflation forecasts for 15 of 21 developed economies covered. That suggests inflation worries are spreading and affecting economies that typically experience low price pressures. Cumulatively, median forecasts for 2027 inflation over the past three quarterly polls have risen by 0.7 per centage points for Britain, 0.5 per centage points for the euro zone and only 0.2 per centage points so far for the US. They have risen by 0.4 per centage points for India and by 0.5 per centage point for Brazil. "Higher energy prices continue to ripple through the global economy, but economic activity remains resilient, supported by the AI-led investment cycle and firmer-than-expected activity across several regions," Seth Carpenter, global chief economist at Morgan Stanley, said in a note. "The inflation picture has become more complex as signs of energy pass-through into core measures are beginning to emerge." The effects of rising prices on household budgets have taken centre stage in various political campaigns across the world. Opinion polls show voters ahead of US midterm elections on November 3 are preoccupied with these issues and Brazil's presidential election, which gave incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva his fourth non-consecutive term, was also fought on cost of living issues. In contrast to two previous polls in April and July, which painted a weak-growth, high-inflation scenario, the latest forecasts lean towards one where price pressures accompany more robust economic performance. Economists upgraded their global growth forecasts for both this year and next, to 3.0 per cent and 3.2 per cent, respectively, from 2.9 per cent and 3.1 per cent in the July poll, though the 2027 forecast is lower than the 3.4 per cent the International Monetary Fund is predicting. The US, which leads in AI capital expenditure that has now become the main driver of domestic growth, is forecast to expand 2.3 per cent this year and 2.1 per cent in 2027. (Corrects spelling of analyst's name in paragraph 4) By Dan Catchpole and Shivansh Tiwary SEATTLE, Oct 27 : Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg said on Tuesday that the company will miss its 737 production and jet delivery targets this year, dealing a setback to its recovery and sending shares tumbling nearly 10 per cent, their worst day in more than 18 months. The company also said it expects free cash flow to grow slower than analysts expected, reaching its $10 billion target in 2029, a year later than investors' consensus, according to LSEG data.

While many aerospace companies are struggling to increase output, Boeing is recovering from years of crises and controversies that dented its reputation, drained cash and saddled it with a heavy debt load. That may make investors more inclined to sell shares, even though Boeing's long-term outlook remains good due to high demand for jetliners and only one major competitor, Europe's Airbus, said Tony Bancroft, an investment analyst with Gabelli Funds investment group. The market is going to punish any delay in increasing cash flow, he said. Boeing expects to generate $3 billion next year, lower than Wall Street's consensus projection of $5.5 billion due to lower deliveries and higher capital investment, Jefferies analyst Sheila Kahyaoglu said in a research note on Tuesday. The company posted free cash flow of $464 million in the most recent quarter; for the year so far it has burned through $359 million in cash, but it still expects to generate $2 billion by the end of the year. Boeing reported an adjusted loss of 34 cents per share for the quarter through September, compared with an expected loss of 21 cents, according to data compiled by LSEG. Shares were down 9.6 per cent to $170.23 in afternoon trading, which would be the stock's worst day since April 3, 2025. PRODUCTION STRUGGLES Boeing now expects to reach its 737 production rate target of 47 jets a month in early 2027. As recently as May, Boeing executives said they would hit that pace this summer. As a result, Boeing will not reach its 500-jet delivery target this year, the company's financial chief Jay Malave said during a conference call with analysts on Tuesday. Wing production continues to be a major constraint, but Boeing still plans to increase to 52 jets a month in the second half of 2027, Ortberg said on the call. To reach that rate, Boeing needs to be producing five jets a month at its new 737 production line in Everett, Washington, which opened in July, and increase fuselage production at the former Spirit AeroSystems plant in Wichita, Kansas. Boeing bought Spirit last year in part due to significant ongoing manufacturing defects. Currently, Boeing is making fuselages at a lower rate while it uses up its existing inventory. Starting now, it has to increase output at Wichita to be in line with 737 output, Ortberg said. Deliveries of the popular single-aisle jetliner are a major driver of Boeing's cash flow, and before Ortberg joined Boeing in 2024, the company had struggled for years with production problems due to rushing rate increases at the expense of quality. Despite pressure to increase 737 output faster, "we're going to be smart about this, stay disciplined, and the outlook is there," Ortberg said. The company continues to struggle with production challenges in its 787 program and a supplier dispute has stalled wing production for 777 freighters and 767s, which includes the KC-46 aerial refueling tanker, as first reported by Reuters on Friday. Shipments for wing production have resumed, but the disruption will show up "over the next few quarters," Malave said. Boeing expects the 777-9 jetliner will be on track for regulator certification by mid-2027, with 10 to 15 deliveries next year. LARGER-THAN-EXPECTED QUARTERLY LOSS The dimmer outlook and a larger-than-expected quarterly loss overshadowed major wins by Boeing in recent months: certification by US regulators of the 737 MAX 7 and MAX 10 and winning the US Navy's sixth-generation F/A-XX fighter contract. "Expectations are rising, and they should. We have a stronger foundation than a year ago, but we also have more work to do to deliver on our backlog, strengthen our culture, and improve how we work every day," Ortberg said in a memo to employees after the results. Revenue at Boeing's commercial airplanes division dipped slightly to $10.7 billion, while the operating loss stood at $697 million for an operating margin of negative 6.5 per cent, compared with negative 48.3 per cent a year ago. The company attributed the performance to less profitable jetliner deliveries and higher production costs, including from its supply chain. At Boeing's defense division, higher deliveries, improved operational performance and a $252-million sale of subsidiary HRL Laboratories contributed to nearly $500 million in quarterly earnings with an operating margin of 6.2 per cent, up from 1.7 per cent a year ago. Boeing Global Services earned $1 billion and posted an operating margin of 18.3 per cent. The US planemaker ended the quarter with $25.2 billion in net debt, down slightly from $25.9 billion at the close of the previous quarter and $30.4 billion a year ago.

Source: Reuters
